selected.hook_line: If nakedness itself causes shame, why did this statue need a removable fig leaf?
selected.viewer_expectation: If exposed genitals are inherently shameful, the statue should always have needed covering.
selected.visible_contradiction: A nude David cast stands uncovered while its custom plaster fig leaf rests separately beside it.
selected.frame_zero: The full nude David cast and the detached plaster fig leaf are visible together at once.
selected.character_action: She points from the unused leaf to David, then closes her long fingers around her orb.
selected.reaction: A dry side-eye at the leaf, then a restrained crooked grin.
selected.activity: Testing whether the objection belonged to the body or to a changing rule.
selected.location: Quiet sculpture-cast gallery beside a full-scale David replica.
selected.topic_link: The body stayed the same while the rule about acceptable exposure changed.
selected.factual_anchor: V&A: its 1857 David cast had a proportional fig leaf made after Queen Victoria reportedly objected to the nudity; it was later hung for royal visits.
selected.payoff: Shame around nakedness is not just a skin reflex; social rules help define when exposure feels improper.

entry_bridge.a_end: Her fingers settle on the orb as it reflects David and the detached leaf in one curved image.
entry_bridge.b_start: Tight orb reflection framed by her long fingers and moss-green sleeve.
entry_bridge.reveal: The covering was added later, so acceptability changed without the body changing.
entry_bridge.world_entry: Host-free museum reenactment: David's cast stands nude while the commissioned plaster fig leaf waits nearby.
